Thanks Alyssa — got the snapshot and shared with ops/tech. Quick answers up front:

- Crediting model: we typically propose a blended credits package for pilots — a guaranteed monthly credit that covers baseline consumption + a burst pool for spikes. That lets you keep predictable unit economics while we instrument caching/kv effectiveness.
- Discounts: for 12-month reserved capacity we can offer a tiered discount (higher effective %) depending on commit bands; I can sketch two scenarios (conservative and aggressive).
- Risks w/ aggressive KV caching + 4-bit quant: generally low if you validate quality on your prompt set; main risks are occasional token-level drop in fidelity and slightly different latency profiles on cold starts. We'll bake in rollback logic and QA gates.

Connor and Priya — can you review the attached snapshot and propose: (1) an initial credits sketch (monthly base + burst), (2) a quantization recommendation with fallback policy, and (3) a short ops checklist for deployment?

I'll assemble a one-page commercial that leadership can review.

Alyssa, Marissa — reviewed the CSV. Quick technical sketch below (short bullets):

- Baseline sizing: your averages (128 tokens/gen) map well to our T4-equivalent footprints. 2M tokens/month baseline = small cluster; handle spikes with burst pool.
- Batching: use adaptive batching with a 40ms max wait window for user-facing calls to keep p95 under target. For embeddings, shard across 4 workers to parallelize throughput.
- KV caching suggestions: enable prefix caching for the top 500 prompt templates (you'll get ~18-24% token reduction initially). TTLs: 6h for user-session prefixes, 30m for ephemeral prompts.
- Quantization: recommend a staged rollout — start with 8-bit quant on a shadowed slice of traffic (10%), hold quality eval for 72h, then 4-bit on a smaller traffic slice (2%) if metrics OK. Provide an automated fallback to 8-bit or FP16 on quality regressions.
- Measurement: instrument token-level perplexity delta, embed cosine drift, and production SLOs (latency + error rates).

Commercially, caching gives the largest predictable savings; quant lowers unit GPU cost but requires quality gating. Priya: I'll need an estimated savings model (tokens saved vs. percent quant adoption) to feed Marissa's commercial.

Connor

Alyssa — attached is a one-page commercial sketch plus a technical annex (see attachments and HubSpot link below). Summary of the two bands we discussed:

1) Conservative pilot (low risk)
- Commitment: 12 months guaranteed credit covering 2M tokens/month baseline
- Burst: 50% monthly burst pool (pay-as-you-go beyond that)
- Unit concession: 10% off hosted token rate on baseline usage
- Ops: enable adaptive batching + prefix caching for top 150 templates (we'll start there, not 500)
- Quant: pilot 8-bit on 10% traffic for 2 weeks, measure; 4-bit only if no material quality regressions

2) Aspirational pilot (higher savings)
- Commitment: 12 months, baseline credit + 100% burst pool
- Unit concession: 15% off hosted token rate on baseline usage + one-time migration credit of $10k to offset quant validation work
- Ops: aggressive caching (top 500) + staged 4-bit rollout with auto-fallback rules
- Quality SLA: automated rollback on embed cosine drift > 0.08 or token-level perplexity delta > 6%

Next steps:
- Procurement: confirm which band (conservative vs aspirational) you want to present to leadership.
- Tech: Connor & Priya will provide the savings model and a one-page ops checklist.
